title: Separate secure connectivity from security-service enforcement
explanation: SASE combines WAN connectivity capabilities, commonly SD-WAN, with cloud-delivered security services. SSE describes the security-services portion without requiring that WAN transport component. Typical security capabilities include secure web gateways, cloud access security broker functions and zero-trust application access. Labels alone do not establish which flows are inspected, where policy is enforced or what happens during an outage. SD-WAN can select paths according to application and measured link conditions across different transport providers, but application awareness is not equivalent to decrypting and inspecting every transaction. Zero trust requires explicit identity, device and authorization decisions rather than automatically trusting an internal address. In a scenario, identify the user, application, enforcement point and permitted path, then test whether traffic can bypass controls through direct Internet access, another tunnel or an unmanaged device.

title: Use infrastructure as code without blindly overwriting drift
explanation: Infrastructure as code describes intended infrastructure or configuration in versioned files that tools can apply repeatedly. Templates and reusable tasks reduce inconsistent manual work; dynamic inventories discover changing targets instead of relying on an obsolete host list. A plan or diff is evidence of proposed changes, not proof those changes are safe. Configuration drift occurs when live state differs from the intended version, perhaps because of an emergency repair or an unauthorized edit. Investigate the reason before restoring a baseline: blindly applying an old template could remove a needed correction. Version control preserves history, branches isolate work and review exposes conflicts, but a textual merge does not prove two network policies remain compatible. Keep secrets outside ordinary source files, validate target inventory and dependencies, review effects and retain a recovery path.

title: Choose dual stack, tunneling or NAT64 deliberately
explanation: IPv6 transition approaches solve different compatibility problems. Dual stack runs IPv4 and IPv6 on participating devices, requiring routing, name resolution, firewall policy and monitoring for both families. A device can prefer a broken IPv6 path even while its IPv4 path works, so test each family explicitly. Tunneling carries one protocol inside another across a network that lacks native support; encapsulation adds overhead and does not automatically provide encryption. NAT64 translates between IPv6 clients and IPv4 services, commonly paired with DNS64 synthesis of IPv6 answers from IPv4 records. It is translation, not dual stack on the client. Applications that embed literal IPv4 addresses or carry addresses in payloads can require additional handling. Document the end-to-end requirement and choose a method that meets it rather than assuming IPv6 address abundance eliminates interoperability work.

title: Compare routing protocols without confusing their metrics
explanation: Static routes are explicitly configured and can be appropriate for predictable stub networks, but they need maintenance when topology changes. OSPF is a link-state interior routing protocol that constructs a topology database and calculates paths using cost. EIGRP is an advanced distance-vector interior protocol with its own neighbor and composite-metric behavior. BGP exchanges reachability and path attributes and is central to interdomain routing; policy can matter more than a physically short path. Metrics from different protocols are not interchangeable units. Administrative distance, or an equivalent implementation preference, chooses between route sources for the same prefix; a protocol's metric ranks its candidates. Forwarding then uses the longest matching installed prefix. When a route is missing, check neighbor relationships, advertisement, filters and next-hop reachability before treating the metric as the only cause.

title: Separate gateway redundancy from VLAN subinterfaces

Subinterfaces divide a physical routed interface into logical interfaces, commonly associated with separate 802.1Q VLAN tags in router-on-a-stick designs. Each VLAN needs appropriate addressing and routing policy. This separates broadcast domains but shares physical capacity and failure dependencies. A subinterface is not the same as a switch virtual interface, which represents a VLAN's layer-3 interface on a switch.

explanation: An SVI gives a VLAN an IP interface for management or routing, depending on device capability and configuration. A phone-plus-PC access port can place voice and data into distinct VLANs using the platform's voice-VLAN behavior; verify both device tagging and switch settings. Spanning tree prevents layer-2 loops by selecting a root and controlling forwarding paths. On non-root switches, the root port is the best path toward the root; a designated port wins forwarding responsibility on a segment, and alternate ports provide non-forwarding alternatives in rapid spanning tree. MTU is a separate compatibility concern: jumbo frames require suitable support along the complete path. A link can be forwarding and correctly tagged while discarding oversized frames.

title: Distinguish SSIDs, radio identities, modes and antennas
explanation: An SSID is the human-facing network name. Roaming requires more than matching names: security, VLAN or mobility handling and client decisions must support continuity. Infrastructure mode connects clients through APs; ad hoc links peers without a conventional infrastructure AP, while point-to-point links commonly join two fixed locations. Mesh can use wireless backhaul, consuming airtime and depending on upstream mesh paths. Omnidirectional antennas distribute energy around a coverage area; directional antennas concentrate it toward a target. Antenna gain reshapes radiation rather than creating unlimited transmitter power, and alignment, polarization and local limits matter.

title: Read SNMP versions, object counters and event notifications
explanation: SNMP managers query agents using object identifiers whose structure and meaning are defined in MIB modules. SNMPv3 supports security modes with authentication and privacy, but selecting version 3 alone does not prove encryption: configure and verify the intended authenticated, encrypted mode. Polling asks for current values; traps are unsolicited notifications and can be lost. An inform requests acknowledgment. Combine events with periodic polling and other evidence. title: Choose API, mirror, flow and discovery evidence
explanation: Monitoring methods reveal different slices of network behavior. A device API can retrieve structured state or change configuration, so authenticate it, scope permissions and handle pagination, rate limits and partial failure. A successful first response does not prove that every device or interface was collected. Port mirroring copies selected traffic to an observation destination; capture accuracy depends on direction, VLAN selection, switch behavior and whether the mirror destination can keep up. Oversubscription can drop observed copies even when production forwarding succeeds. Flow records summarize conversations and counters but ordinarily do not contain complete application payloads. Discovery identifies responding devices through specific methods and permissions; silence can mean filtering or unsupported discovery rather than absence. Align timestamps, sampling windows and baselines before correlating sources. Protect captured data because copied packets and management responses can contain sensitive information.

title: Calculate reliability metrics and evaluate recovery-site readiness
explanation: MTTR describes the average repair or restoration interval under the organization's defined measurement method; MTBF describes average operating time between failures for repairable systems. Neither is the same as a maximum permitted outage or a guarantee about the next failure. Under a simplified steady-state model, availability is MTBF divided by MTBF plus MTTR, but real service availability also depends on dependencies, planned downtime and the measurement definition. A cold recovery site supplies limited facilities and requires substantial setup. A warm site has some prepared systems or data but still needs activation work. A hot site is more ready for operation, yet failover, data consistency, identity, network access and staffing still require validation. Active-active shares service across operating instances; active-passive reserves a standby role. Test actual dependencies against recovery objectives.

title: Read DNS roles, zones and record-specific evidence
explanation: A forward zone maps names to records such as IPv4 A and IPv6 AAAA addresses; a reverse zone uses PTR records for address-to-name lookup and is administered separately. Creating one direction does not automatically create the other. CNAME identifies an alias to another name, MX selects mail exchangers, TXT stores application-defined text, and NS identifies authoritative name servers. A primary zone is the source for its configured secondary copies; a secondary remains authoritative for the zone it serves. Recursive resolvers perform or coordinate lookups and cache results, so a non-authoritative cached answer is not automatically untrustworthy. TTL controls caching lifetime rather than propagation instantaneously. A hosts-file entry can override normal DNS behavior on a client. Query the relevant record, server and context before deciding that a successful A lookup proves mail or reverse DNS works.

title: Separate DNS authenticity from encrypted resolver transport
explanation: DNSSEC authenticates signed DNS data using a validation chain and detects unauthorized changes to covered records. It does not encrypt query names or prevent an authorized zone owner from publishing a bad address. DNS over TLS protects the client-to-resolver transport with TLS, commonly on TCP 853; DNS over HTTPS carries DNS exchanges through HTTPS, commonly on port 443. These transport protections do not by themselves validate a zone's signatures or make a resolver trustworthy. A signed zone with expired signatures or a broken delegation chain can fail validation while an insecure lookup appears to succeed. Diagnose resolver reachability, TLS identity and DNSSEC validation separately rather than disabling validation as the first repair. Enterprise policy must also account for managed clients using alternate encrypted resolvers that can bypass intended filtering or split-horizon DNS.

title: Choose time synchronization and interpret its security limits
explanation: Consistent time supports authentication, certificate validation, log correlation and recovery analysis. NTP distributes time over IP and is widely appropriate for general systems, but a reachable server alone does not prove a client is synchronized or that the source is trustworthy. Examine offset, reachability, source selection and status. PTP targets more precise synchronization in suitable environments and can use hardware timestamping and network elements designed to account for transit timing. It is not simply an NTP server with a lower stratum value. NTS adds cryptographic protection to client-server NTP through TLS-based key establishment and authenticated NTP exchanges. It authenticates timing messages but cannot remove all network-delay effects or magically correct a wrong trusted time source. Choose the accuracy, hardware and trust design required by the application.

title: Compare full, split and clientless remote access
explanation: A site-to-site VPN connects networks through gateways, while a client-to-site VPN connects an individual endpoint into a controlled remote-access environment. Full tunneling routes the intended client traffic through the VPN gateway, allowing centralized inspection but adding bandwidth and latency demands. Split tunneling sends selected destinations through the tunnel while other traffic follows local access, so route scope, DNS behavior and endpoint exposure need explicit design. A clientless VPN commonly provides browser-based access to supported web applications through a portal or proxy; it does not guarantee arbitrary protocol access or replace every installed VPN client. Encryption protects the tunnel segment, not necessarily the endpoint or every onward application hop. Evaluate authentication, allowed routes, DNS, endpoint posture and authorization independently. A connected tunnel indicator is only the beginning of a successful application test.

title: Distinguish SSO assertions from device-administration AAA
explanation: SSO lets a user authenticate through an identity system and access permitted applications without repeating independent logins at each one. Federation crosses trust boundaries using agreed assertions or tokens; SAML is one framework for exchanging such assertions. The receiving service must validate signatures, issuer, audience, validity interval and context rather than trusting any token-shaped message. SSO does not automatically make every application authorized. RADIUS commonly supports network-access AAA, while TACACS+ is widely used for network-device administration and can separate authentication, authorization and accounting operations. A successful login should not grant every command; role or command authorization limits actions, and accounting records what occurred. Time-based codes require clock alignment and resist different threats from phishing-resistant cryptographic authentication. Plan controlled fallback access so an identity-server outage does not silently result in unrestricted administration.

title: Connect risk, CIA goals and data-location obligations
explanation: A vulnerability is a weakness, a threat is a potentially harmful circumstance or actor, and an exploit is a means of taking advantage of a weakness. Risk combines the likelihood and impact of harmful outcomes in the relevant environment; a severe weakness on an isolated test machine and the same weakness on an exposed payment system can create different priorities. Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure, integrity protects against unauthorized modification and availability supports timely authorized access. Security controls often support several goals but may trade them off during an incident. Compliance requirements need a defined scope, data inventory, accountable owners and evidence. Data locality concerns where data resides or is processed; geographic restrictions do not by themselves encrypt or authenticate it. PCI DSS and GDPR have different scopes and obligations, so identify applicability rather than treating either as a universal network certification.

title: Recognize MAC flooding, poisoned resolution and VLAN abuse
explanation: MAC flooding attempts to exhaust a switch's forwarding-table resources through many source addresses, potentially increasing unknown-unicast flooding. It does not guarantee every switch reveals all traffic; platform behavior, limits and segmentation matter. ARP poisoning supplies false address-to-MAC mappings on a local IPv4 network and can redirect or disrupt traffic. DNS poisoning targets name-to-data answers or caches at a different layer, so inspect resolver and validation evidence rather than treating all redirection as ARP. VLAN hopping can exploit unintended trunk negotiation or specific tagging/native-VLAN conditions. Defenses should address the mechanism: restrict access-port behavior, allow only intended VLANs, control source-MAC learning and apply DHCP snooping with correctly configured dynamic ARP inspection where supported. Capture and compare authoritative mappings before concluding that a changing MAC is necessarily malicious; legitimate failover also changes ownership.

DNS poisoning: False name-resolution data.

title: Trace social engineering and malware through network consequences
explanation: Social engineering manipulates people into disclosing information or performing unsafe actions; phishing uses deceptive messages, while pretexting invents a believable role or situation. A fake support caller requesting a reset can bypass technical controls if staff skip verification. Malware describes malicious software, with effects that may include credential theft, lateral movement, botnet participation, ransomware or resource consumption. A network symptom is evidence, not a complete malware diagnosis: repeated failed connections could also be a broken application or misconfigured monitor. Correlate endpoint evidence, identity events and network destinations before assigning cause. Defenses combine independent verification, least privilege, segmentation, endpoint controls, tested recovery and reporting. A honeypot or honeynet is a deliberately monitored deception environment, not an ordinary production service or a guarantee that every attacker will interact with it.

title: Harden management, filtering and key lifecycle at real boundaries
explanation: Hardening reduces unnecessary exposure through supported firmware, secure management protocols, changed defaults, disabled unused services and least-privilege administration. Filtering must specify source, destination, service and direction at the boundary where unwanted traffic actually crosses. A DMZ exposes selected services between controlled zones; it is not automatically trusted or safe because of its name. IoT, guest, BYOD and operational-technology networks need explicit permitted flows rather than unlimited mutual access. OT changes also require coordination with safety and availability owners. Wireless MAC filtering and hidden SSIDs are weak identity controls because identifiers can be observed or imitated. Keys and certificates require secure generation, storage, distribution, rotation, revocation and recovery; replacing a certificate without updating trust or renewing it before expiry can create an outage. Validate intended allowed and denied flows after every change.

title: Interpret interface counters and port states before replacing hardware
explanation: Interface state and error counters describe different failures. Administratively down usually means configuration intentionally disables an interface; operational down suggests no usable physical or protocol link, while an error-disabled state can reflect a protective policy response. CRC or FCS errors indicate damaged received frames but do not uniquely identify a bad cable; investigate media, optics, interference and negotiation. Runts, giants and discards need platform definitions because counters and included frame sizes vary. Increasing output discards can indicate queue congestion rather than physical corruption. Compare counter deltas during the failure with speed, duplex, utilization and recent changes. A historical nonzero counter may predate the incident. Transceiver readings, cable tests and known-good substitutions can strengthen a hypothesis, but avoid disconnecting production links without an authorized change and recovery plan.

A captive portal can block useful traffic after association, so successful Wi-Fi connection is not equivalent to completed access. Packet captures and controller events help identify authentication or roaming delays but have collection limits. Compare a stationary baseline with the moving-client symptom before changing every AP.

title: Choose cellular and satellite links from measured service needs
explanation: Cellular WAN uses a carrier radio network and suitable modem, subscription and antenna arrangement. Coverage bars alone do not establish throughput: radio quality, congestion, band support, carrier policy and backhaul affect performance. Satellite can extend connectivity where terrestrial options are unavailable, but requires an appropriate terminal, view of the sky, service coverage and power. Geostationary systems have substantial propagation delay because of orbital distance; lower-orbit systems can reduce that distance but still vary with routing, obstruction, weather and handovers. Neither technology guarantees a public inbound-reachable address; carrier-grade NAT and provider policy may affect remote access. Compare latency, jitter, loss, throughput, data limits and recovery behavior against application requirements. A backup circuit should be tested with representative traffic and independent dependencies rather than accepted because its link indicator is green.

title: Read Category 7, Category 8 and shielding claims correctly
explanation: Cable marketing can obscure the standard for the complete channel. Category 8 targets short data-center channels, commonly up to 30 meters, supporting 25GBASE-T and 40GBASE-T with compatible equipment and channel construction. It does not extend those rates to every 100-meter office run. Shielded twisted pair can reduce certain interference when properly installed and bonded, but poor shield handling is not a substitute for correct routing and termination. Compare the required application, channel standard and certification result rather than assuming a larger category number fixes every fault.

title: Diagnose suspended aggregation members without creating loops

LACP negotiation and compatibility checks are separate from cable continuity. Check whether both peers expect dynamic negotiation, whether an active participant initiates it and whether the observed partner is the intended device. Two passive participants may not initiate an exchange. Member settings such as speed, VLAN trunk policy and aggregation configuration must satisfy platform consistency rules. A static bundle on one end and LACP on the other can create a mismatch rather than useful redundancy. Do not force an individual member to forward merely to remove a suspended indicator: that can bypass safety behavior or introduce a loop. title: Distinguish physical social attacks from location-based controls
explanation: Physical access controls protect equipment and information when network authentication is not the first boundary. Tailgating follows an authorized person through a controlled entrance without separate authorization. Shoulder surfing observes passwords or other sensitive information from a nearby position or view. Dumpster diving retrieves useful information or media from discarded material. These mechanisms need different practical responses: independent entry authorization, privacy-aware work areas and secure disposal. Locks, cameras and visitor records can support prevention or investigation, but a camera does not itself prevent entry or prove that someone is authorized. Geofencing uses a location condition as part of policy, such as allowing access only in a defined area. Location can be imprecise or manipulated and should not replace identity, device health and authorization. Evaluate the actual evidence and required response rather than assuming familiar appearance means trusted access.

Shoulder surfing: Observing sensitive information from a viewing position.
Dumpster diving: Recovering information from discarded materials.

title: Separate URL filtering, content filtering and certificate trust
explanation: URL filtering controls access based on requested addresses, categories or policy lists, while content filtering examines content characteristics according to the inspection available. Encryption changes visibility: an observer may see a destination address or some connection metadata without seeing a complete HTTPS URL or body. Do not claim that a basic IP ACL filters every encrypted page path. TLS inspection introduces a trusted intermediary and requires deliberate certificate deployment, authorized policy and compatibility testing. A self-signed certificate signs itself rather than chaining to a separately trusted issuer. It can support encrypted communication when explicitly and safely trusted, but accepting any warning does not establish server identity. Publicly issued certificates also require correct hostname, validity and chain checks. Separate trust failure from filtering denial so that an access repair does not remove the protection the policy intended.

title: Choose physical tools, discovery and command output by the question
explanation: A toner and probe help identify a cable among terminations; they do not certify its maximum Ethernet performance. A cable tester may check continuity and wire map, while a suitable certifier evaluates performance against a cabling standard. A visual fault locator sends visible light through fiber to help locate continuity, polarity or accessible break problems; it is not a complete optical loss certification and requires laser-safe handling. A network tap copies traffic from a selected link with installation and optical/electrical considerations. LLDP and CDP advertise neighboring-device information on local links, but absent or disabled discovery does not prove no neighbor exists. On hosts, netstat or equivalent socket tools show local listeners and sessions; on switches, interface, MAC, ARP, VLAN, route, configuration and power commands answer distinct questions. Nmap reports observations from a scan method and vantage point, not an absolute universal service inventory.

title: Size DHCP leases and distinguish reservations from exclusions
explanation: A DHCP scope defines the addresses and options a server can allocate for a subnet. An exclusion removes selected addresses from dynamic allocation, commonly to avoid conflicts with deliberately static assignments. A reservation associates a stable assignment with a client identifier according to the server's implementation; it still relies on DHCP rather than configuring the address statically on the client. Lease duration affects address reuse and renewal traffic. Long leases can retain addresses for departed transient devices and contribute to pool exhaustion, while very short leases increase renewal activity and dependence on timely service. A relay forwards appropriate client messages between subnets, but the server must select a matching scope and return useful options. Changing the lease alone does not fix the wrong subnet, insufficient capacity, duplicate static assignments or a broken relay. Measure active usage, churn and failed allocations before choosing a repair.
distinctions: Scope: Subnet-specific allocation range and options.
Exclusion: Addresses withheld from dynamic allocation.
Reservation: Stable DHCP assignment tied to client identification.
